title: Auditlog storage compact indexing strategy and backfill checklist
content:
Purpose and scope
This note captures the proposed compact indexing strategy and operational checklist for audit log storage, retention tiers, and common backfill paths. It is intended for the security, infra, and SRE teams who operate the audit ingestion and indexing pipelines and for product/console owners who rely on historical audit evidence. It intentionally focuses on implementation and failure-mode handling rather than policy text.

Background and constraints
- Audit logs are high-cardinality, high-throughput events: auth attempts, API calls, admin actions, RBAC v2 grants/revokes, evidence snapshots.
- Logs must be retained for multiple retention tiers: short-term (30d) for fast search, medium-term (1y) for investigations, and long-term (7y) for compliance (evidence blobs moved to cold storage).
- Query latency SLO: sub-500ms for hot tier searches, <2s for medium-tier aggregations with cache, and best-effort for cold restores.
- Storage cost must be controlled; index footprint should be minimized while preserving useful sort/filter fields for investigations and SIEM exports.

Goals
1) Provide a compact indexed representation for hot/medium tiers that supports typical security queries (principal, resource, action, timestamp, request_id, outcome, IP).
2) Keep cold-tier raw blobs retrievable with verified integrity (hash).
3) Make backfills and re-indexing predictable, resumable, and idempotent.
4) Ensure clear runbooks for failure modes to minimize investigation downtime.

Retention tiers and storage classes (recommended)
- Hot (0-30d): Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (sharded time-based indices) or RediSearch for extremely hot slices. Full compact index with pre-computed derived fields (principal_normalized, outcome_code). 
- Warm (31-365d): compressed index store (fewer replicas, larger shards) optimized for scan queries and aggregated searches.
- Cold (1y-7y): object store (S3/GCS) containing compressed raw events + minimal index metadata (key -> object path + hash). Cold retrieval is async and routed via the private control plane.
- Archive (7y+): long-term immutable archive bucket with legal hold support.

Indexing strategy (compact index model)
- Minimal indexed fields (strings normalized, enums): timestamp, tenant_id, principal_id, action_type, resource_id, request_id, correlation_id, outcome (enum), ip_address (anonymized prefix/hash for PII control), device_id, geo_region, event_version, schema_hash.
- No-op: avoid indexing full request/response bodies in hot indices. Store large payloads in object store and reference by UUID.
- Use time-based indices with daily rollover for hot tier (index name: audit-compact-YYYY.MM.DD). Warm tier uses monthly indices or migrated shards.
- Sharding: target 20–40GB primary shard size after compression. Adjust shard count by incoming events per day per cluster. Use tenant-aware routing keys for high-volume customers to avoid hot shards.
- Mapping: strongly typed fields for enums and keywords; disable indexing on free-text fields except a single summary field with analyzers for ad-hoc text search.
- Compression: enable best-effort doc_values compression and source filtering for hot/warm tiers.

Pipeline overview (components)
1) Ingest Kafka topic (audit-raw): producer -> topic partitioning by tenant_id.
2) Validator & enrich service: consumes audit-raw, validates schema (audit schema v2), enriches with derived fields (geo, principal_normalized), emits to audit-enriched topic. Invalid events go to audit-deadletter topic with error metadata.
3) Indexer workers: batch from audit-enriched, apply compact transform (drop/replace heavy fields), write to hot index and optionally to object store for payloads. Index writes are idempotent using request_id + event_version as upsert keys.
4) Archiver: periodic job that compacts and moves index segments from hot -> warm -> cold storage and writes a minimal index manifest to the cold-store-index catalog.
5) SIEM export bridge: subscribes to audit-enriched, applies export mapping and forwards to external SIEM (syslog/sysinf).

Backfill patterns and implementation notes
- Replay-from-topic backfill (preferred when raw topic is retained):
  - Preconditions: retention of audit-raw >= backfill window OR snapshot of raw events persisted.
  - Approach: start a dedicated backfill consumer group that reads from the earliest offset for the desired window, passes events through validator/enricher + indexer. Use idempotent writes and request_id dedupe to avoid double-indexing.
  - Pros: preserves original event order per partition, simple.
  - Cons: depends on raw topic retention; can cause consumer lag and increased cluster load.

- Snapshot-and-replay (for very old windows where raw topic expired):
  - Preconditions: we maintain cold-store snapshots by day (compressed JSONL).
  - Approach: run an offline rehydration job that streams archived snapshots into the validator/enricher path or directly into a reindexer service. Add a slowdown and pacing feature to avoid cluster overload.
  - Pros: does not depend on Kafka retention.
  - Cons: requires reliable snapshots and checksum verification.

- Reindex-from-index (when schema change or mapping fixes required):
  - Use the existing indices as source, extract minimal fields, apply transform, write to new indices with new mapping. This is heavier on search cluster; prefer snapshot -> reindex path.

Idempotency and ordering guarantees
- Use composite id key: tenant_id + request_id + event_version. Indexer should write with op_type=update/upsert and check version if event_version present.
- Deduplication window: for rare duplicate events, dedupe in indexer by hashing payload and storing payload_hash in index metadata.
- For ordering-sensitive sequences (RBAC grants/revokes), ensure consumer grouping by tenant and per-resource ordering semantics are documented; when replays occur, the validator should reject events older than last_seen_version if the target index stores last_applied_version.

Failure modes and mitigation/runbook (top prioritized)
1) Consumer lag spikes (validation or indexer backlog)
   - Symptoms: consumer lag > 2h, hot index ingestion falls behind, SIEM export delay.
   - Immediate action: scale indexer consumer group (k8s replica bump), increase consumer parallelism, temporarily enable bulk-index low-latency mode (smaller batches) if memory pressure high.
   - If scaling fails: start targeted backfill windowing (fast-forward policy) and alert impacted teams.

2) Corrupt payloads / schema drift
   - Symptoms: validator errors increase, entries land in audit-deadletter, indexer errors.
   - Immediate action: inspect sample deadletter messages, identify schema change candidate, patch validator schema or run migration. Route critical events into emergency bypass with a special transformer that normalizes missing fields to safe defaults.

3) Index shard failures / split-brain
   - Symptoms: repeated primary shard relocations, high Search/Indexing latency, write rejections.
   - Immediate action: follow SRE index-failure runbook: move indices to recovery nodes, increase replicas to allow relocation, throttle indexing, open P1 incident. If index corruption is suspected, snapshot current state and restore latest healthy snapshot to a new index and switch alias.

4) Backfill job fails mid-window
   - Symptoms: backfill job crashes, partial writes, large consumer lag on reingestion topic.
   - Immediate action: stop job, capture job checkpoint offsets, run verification script that checks idempotency keys for the attempted window, resume from last consistent checkpoint. If checkpoint unavailable, re-run from start of smallest safe sub-window.

5) Cold-store retrieval errors (missing object or hash mismatch)
   - Symptoms: cold retrieval job reports missing object, manifests show mismatched checksums.
   - Immediate action: try alternate replica bucket (cross-region), verify bucket lifecycle policy, if object missing, escalate to legal/compliance and attempt partial reconstruction using neighboring day snapshots.

Operational checklist: pre-backfill
- Verify retention policy and that raw-topic or snapshots cover the target window.
- Confirm index mappings and target index names.
- Reserve cluster capacity (increase indexing throttles, open maintenance window).
- Notify downstream consumers (SIEM, console teams) of temporary increased latencies.
- Snapshot current affected indices.
- Run dry-run on a small sample window and validate results.

Backfill run checklist
- Run backfill with windowing of at most 24h per job for safety.
- Track offsets and write a durable checkpoint to the control plane for resume.
- Monitor consumer lag, indexing error rate, and index growth.
- On job completion: run checksum diff between expected by-day counts and actual indexed counts; produce a reconciliation report to security owner.

Monitoring, alerts and dashboards
- Alerts: consumer_lag_seconds > 3600 (P1), indexing_error_rate > 1% sustained 5m (P1), index_disk_utilization > 85% (P1), deadletter_rate > 0.1% for > 30m (P2), cold_retrieval_error_rate > 0.1% (P2).
- Dashboards: hot/warm index ingestion TPS, compact-index size per day, average query p95 latencies, backfill progress panel (jobs in progress, offsets, throughput), SIEM export success rate.

Testing checklist (pre-merge / pre-rollout)
- Unit tests for compact transform that assert required fields and that heavy payloads are referenced not inlined.
- Integration test that replays a synthetic 72-hour window into indexer and validates counts and idempotency.
- Chaos test: kill an indexer pod mid-batch and validate resume from checkpoint and no duplicates.
- Cold retrieval test: restore a random archived day and validate object integrity and search result equality to historical snapshot.

SIEM export considerations
- Map compact fields to SIEM schema; ensure anonymized_ip is used where PII policy demands.
- Export pace-limiting: SIEM endpoints typically rate-limit—bridge must support backoff with durable queueing.
- Ensure exports can be replayed from audit-enriched topic without touching hot indices.

RBAC v2 interactions
- RBAC events (grant/revoke) are sensitive for ordering. Store grant state snapshots in a tiny key-value store (per-tenant) so that replays can detect stale/grant-ordering mismatches.
- Audit entries for role changes should include pre_state and post_state references in cold store; compact index stores only change summary and reference id.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Determine exact shelf-life for audit-enriched Kafka topics vs cost of raw snapshots.
- Decide if we provide per-tenant TTL overrides (some customers require longer hot indexing window).
- Evaluate RediSearch for sub-second single-tenant lookups vs OpenSearch for cross-tenant analytics.

Appendix: quick commands and helper scripts
- Check consumer lag: kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server x:9092 --describe --group audit-indexer
- Resume backfill from checkpoint: ./tools/backfill-runner --from-offset X --to-offset Y --checkpoint /mnt/checkpoints/window-YYYYMMDD.json
- Verify index doc counts: curl -s "http://es.cluster/_cat/indices/audit-compact-*?v&s=index" | awk '{sum += $7} END {print sum }'
- Reindex snapshot to new mapping (high level): 1) restore snapshot to temp cluster 2) run transform 3) bulk reindex to production index alias.

Summary
This document captures a compact-index-first approach that minimizes hot index footprint, keeps raw payloads in cold storage, and makes backfills reproducible and resumable. The emphasis is on idempotent writes and checkpoints so we can perform replays without affecting RBAC ordering guarantees or SIEM exports. The operational checklists and failure runbooks are intended to reduce mean-time-to-recovery for common ingestion/indexing failures.

If approved, next steps: formalize SLA/retention tables with product and legal, add a small RFC for shard sizing by tenant, and schedule a dry-run backfill for a two-week window to validate pacing defaults.
